title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
gist: Big Tech-backed power uprates at existing US nuclear plants (Constellation's roughly 1 GW across 11 reactors, Vistra's $4.2B DOE loan for 433 MW) are surging, but the total uprate potential of 3-8 GW is small next to PJM's expected 30 GW of AI-driven peak demand growth by 2030, so new reactors will eventually be needed.

insights.claim: Constellation, the largest US nuclear operator, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of capacity across 11 reactors at six plants, spending more than $4.3 billion on uprates, enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The largest US nuclear operator is investing in capacity additions; monitor Constellation's execution and returns.
insights.locator: Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US

insights.claim: A 20-year agreement under which Google buys electricity from the Constellation plants was a major factor in making the uprates happen, and Constellation's CEO said such projects require a different price point than the market trades at.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler long-term power purchase agreements are what unlock nuclear capex; contracted offtake with premium pricing is the driver.
insights.quote: These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.
insights.locator: Behind it all? Big Tech money

insights.claim: The US Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan on October 5 to Vistra for upgrades at three plants in Pennsylvania and Ohio that will add 433 megawatts, with Meta already signed to buy the electricity in a long-term deal.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Federal financing combined with hyperscaler offtake de-risks nuclear upgrade projects; the loan works out to roughly $9.7M per MW added.
insights.locator: Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra

insights.claim: US NRC approvals of uprates fell from over 80 in 2001-2010 to 33 in 2011-2020 as demand plateaued and cheap natural gas pressured nuclear plants, but AI-driven demand is reversing that trend as shuttered plants such as Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: The AI power-demand shock has revived a dormant nuclear upgrade market; expect higher NRC licensing activity.

insights.claim: Major uprates can boost reactor power by as much as 20% but require replacing equipment such as turbines, pumps, motors, generators and transformers, whereas minor uprates involve changes to instrument setpoints or calculations.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Equipment suppliers for turbines, generators and transformers are potential beneficiaries of the uprate wave.

insights.claim: On a per-kilowatt basis, the Constellation uprate project is cheaper than building a new reactor but still more expensive than a new utility-scale solar farm with storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Uprates are economic only with premium contracted pricing; they are not the cheapest incremental MW.

insights.claim: Of the US nuclear fleet's roughly 98 GW capacity, uprates could add between 3 and 8 GW depending on the estimate, with the NRC already expecting applications to add 2.4 GW through 2032.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Much of the identifiable uprate potential is already in the licensing pipeline, so incremental upside is limited.
insights.locator: Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts

insights.claim: PJM expects about 30 GW of additional peak demand from AI by 2030, so all possible US nuclear uprates would cover only a fraction, and meeting demand with nuclear will eventually require building new reactors.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Uprates are a small, quick bridge; the larger demand gap favors gas, solar plus storage and new-build nuclear for later years.
insights.locator: PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast
